findings.statement: CXCR2 ranks first in convergence, but the verbatim-validated relation set holds no literature relation for it. Abstract chunks do report that CXCR1 and CXCR2 are potential neutrophil extracellular trap-related treatment targets in UC (Mendelian randomization, colocalization, transcriptomics), and that a CXCL5/CXCR2 axis integrating eQTL, pQTL and transcriptome data is tied to neutrophil chemotaxis in UC. These are bioinformatic or genetic-inference studies, not clinical evidence in UC. PubTator3 (machine-extracted) lists UC associations for CXCR2.

The literature links the CXCL8-CXCR1/CXCR2 axis to UC pathogenesis through PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signaling. CXCL8 is also a PPI hub gene in a bioinformatic study. A blood RNA-seq validation (GSE169568) named CXCL8 as a diagnostic gene for IBD (not UC-specific). Evidence is mostly review-level or bioinformatic.

One study reports IDO1 elevated in UC patients and correlated with M1 macrophage polarization in human data and colitis mice. IDO1 induced M1 polarization through the ER stress GRP78-XBP1 pathway, and an IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis. This is a single preclinical study; no clinical IDO1 inhibition in UC is reported here.

CHI3L1 is upregulated in UC patients and correlates with NLRP3 inflammasome expression. It promotes macrophage pyroptosis via BCAT1/NF-kappaB, and NF-kappaB activation reversed the protective effect of CHI3L1 inhibition. Velpatasvir was shown to bind recombinant CHI3L1 in vitro (micromolar affinity), a repurposing signal rather than clinical evidence.

MMP1 is reported as a diagnostic marker (AUC reported in a UC-associated CRC bioinformatic study) and is among transcripts modified by mirikizumab that correlate with Mayo, Geboes and Robarts indices. Ilomastat was only predicted in silico as an MMP1 inhibitor. MMP1 was also positively associated with macrophage infiltration.

DUOX2 protein is among the most elevated in inflamed UC biopsies versus healthy controls, alongside HLA-DRA, CD74 and lipocalin-2. It is listed among eight credible diagnostic or therapeutic biomarkers in a bioinformatic study. Inhibition of DUOX2 overexpression by TLXDS alleviated UC in one study; DUOX2 is also linked to ferroptosis by bioinformatics only.

AQP9 is predominantly expressed in neutrophils and upregulated in colon of UC mice. It promotes NET formation via JAK2-STAT3 pathway-mediated pyroptosis, aggravating epithelial injury. Overexpression was also confirmed by RT-PCR in DSS and anti-CD40 mouse colitis models. The signal is neutrophil-derived and from mouse work. No AQP9 drug is annotated in the ranking.

S100A9 expression showed excellent performance for diagnosing active UC in one study. In tofacitinib-treated UC, S100A9, FCGR3A and MMP12 were downregulated in resident macrophages with response, and the same abstract set reports differential tofacitinib effects on macrophage activation contributing to non-response. S100A9 is a neutrophil/myeloid signal, not epithelial.

CXCL1 appears as a diagnostic gene in several machine-learning or bioinformatic studies, including a modest single-gene AUC in one study and a combined model with other genes in another. It is also overexpressed in pancolitis. Support is bioinformatic only; no therapeutic study is returned.

MMP10 is upregulated in active UC versus remission UC, Crohn's disease and controls, and was elevated in preclinical UC in pre-diagnosis samples. It is listed as a credible diagnostic biomarker in a bioinformatic study. Among the best-replicated biomarker candidates in this corpus, though no therapy is annotated.

SLC26A2 is downregulated in intestinal mucosa of active UC versus healthy controls, correlates with Mayo score and PUCAI, and is negatively correlated with IL-17A. This is a single study; it represents the epithelial loss-of-function arm of the signature.

caveats: CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274, FCGR2A, JAK2, IL2RA, INHBA, TREM1 and CXCL5 have strong expression or Open Targets support but no verbatim-validated literature relation in this corpus (CXCR2 only via abstract chunks and machine-extracted PubTator).
Most literature support for top genes comes from bioinformatic hub-gene or diagnostic-model studies and single preclinical mouse studies; few clinical interventional data are present.
The ranking literature component partly reflects Open Targets literature scores, not this corpus.
Non-UC-specific evidence (IBD-wide blood diagnostic, UC-associated CRC) was used for CXCL8 and MMP1.
No contradictory findings were returned for the genes examined; absence of contradiction reflects corpus size, not consensus.
Numeric values (AUCs) were deliberately described in words because they were not bound to verifiable record fields.
